source: CARDI/MAFF Cashew Disease Management Guide (compiled from 3 sourced technical documents)
text:
Cashew in Cambodia is affected by several fungal diseases.

Collar/root rot: appears in nursery seedlings (in bags or seedbeds). Symptoms: streaking at the base of the stem turning brown to black, spreading to shoots and leaves which wilt and die; white fungal threads visible around the base; roots blacken and rot when the plant is pulled up. Spreads mainly in the rainy season. Prevention: ensure soil is well-leveled and well-drained, sun-dry/solarize soil before use, do not plant seeds too deep, and reduce nitrogen fertilizer use in affected areas.

Fruit rot: caused by a fungus that infects developing fruit from March to July as the fruit begins ripening; fruit turns black and rots, sometimes with a foamy texture; can also affect young fruit, seeds, and flower clusters, causing flowers to drop prematurely. A copper-based fungicide can be used for control -- verify the exact product and dosage rate against the original source before advising a farmer.

Leaf spot: affects trees under 2 years old; small grey spots ringed with reddish-brown, roughly 0.2-2cm across, mainly on older leaves, most common September-December. Severe infestation causes leaves and small branches to dry out and break.

Panicle/flower blight: dries out flower clusters, turning them brown; flowers and any developing fruit drop prematurely; often follows earlier damage from sap-sucking pests like tea mosquito, which create wounds the fungus enters through.

Anthracnose: affects leaves, shoots, flowers, and fruit; on fruit it reduces grain quality and yield; worsens significantly in the rainy season, especially combined with tea mosquito damage, since feeding wounds let the fungus in, and it spreads via wind and rain splash.

Stem/trunk canker: affects the trunk and major branches, disrupting sap flow and weakening flowering, fruiting, and grain quality. Treatment involves cleaning out the affected/damaged bark area thoroughly, then treating the wound with a lime-and-copper-based paste or a systemic treatment -- verify exact mixing ratios against the original source before advising a farmer.

General prevention across all these diseases: good field sanitation (remove and burn infected plant material away from the field), avoid waterlogged soil, prune to allow airflow and sunlight into the canopy, and control sap-sucking pests -- especially tea mosquito -- since their feeding wounds are a common entry point for fungal infection.
